one_liner: Severe RSV illness in infants by 90 days: {{n:sev_vax}} cases after maternal vaccination vs {{n:sev_pbo}} with placebo (efficacy {{n:ve_sev90}}).
one_liner_plain: Vaccinating mothers during pregnancy protected infants from severe RSV illness

citation.title: Bivalent Prefusion F Vaccine in Pregnancy to Prevent RSV Illness in Infants
citation.authors: Kampmann B, Madhi SA, Munjal I, et al.

sections.background: RSV is a leading cause of lower respiratory tract illness and hospitalization in young infants, and the first months of life are the most dangerous. Infants are too young to be vaccinated well themselves, but antibodies made by a vaccinated mother cross the placenta. MATISSE tested whether a single dose of a bivalent RSV prefusion F (RSVpreF) vaccine given during pregnancy could protect newborns through their first months.

methods.design: Phase 3, randomized (1:1), double-blind, placebo-controlled trial in 18 countries; this is the prespecified interim analysis.
methods.population: Healthy pregnant women at 24 through 36 weeks' gestation and their infants. {{n:n_vax}} women received vaccine and {{n:n_pbo}} placebo; {{n:inf_vax}} and {{n:inf_pbo}} infants were evaluated.
methods.intervention: A single intramuscular injection of 120 µg bivalent RSVpreF vaccine (RSV A and B prefusion F proteins).
methods.primary_endpoint: Two primary end points in infants: medically attended severe RSV lower respiratory tract illness, and medically attended RSV lower respiratory tract illness of any severity, each within 90, 120, 150, and 180 days after birth.
methods.follow-up: Infants through 24 months of age for safety (first trial year); efficacy through 180 days and beyond.

sections.results: Within 90 days of birth, medically attended severe RSV lower respiratory tract illness occurred in {{n:sev_vax}} infants in the vaccine group and {{n:sev_pbo}} in the placebo group: vaccine efficacy {{n:ve_sev90}} (99.5% CI 40.6 to 96.3). By 180 days it was {{n:sev180_vax}} versus {{n:sev180_pbo}} cases, efficacy {{n:ve_sev180}}. The second primary end point, RSV lower respiratory tract illness of any severity, fell short: {{n:lrti_vax}} versus {{n:lrti_pbo}} cases within 90 days, efficacy {{n:ve_lrti90}} (99.5% CI 14.7 to 79.8), which did not meet the statistical success criterion. Efficacy against RSV-associated hospitalization was {{n:ve_hosp90}} within 90 days and {{n:ve_hosp180}} within 180 days. No safety signals were detected in mothers or in infants and toddlers up to 24 months. Adverse events within 1 month were similar: {{n:ae_w_vax}} versus {{n:ae_w_pbo}} of women and {{n:ae_i_vax}} versus {{n:ae_i_pbo}} of infants.
sections.conclusions: RSVpreF vaccine given during pregnancy was effective against medically attended severe RSV lower respiratory tract illness in infants, with protection strongest in the first 90 days and still present at 180 days. No safety concerns were identified. Efficacy against RSV illness of any severity did not meet the prespecified success criterion.
sections.limitations: Women with high-risk pregnancies, including those at current risk of preterm birth, with multiple pregnancies, or with a previous infant with a significant congenital anomaly, were excluded, though their babies may be at higher risk of severe RSV. Data from low-income countries, where the vaccine could matter most, were limited. The trial was not powered to compare efficacy by RSV subgroup, and this was an interim analysis.
sections.practice_impact: MATISSE led to the first maternal RSV vaccine (Abrysvo), giving families a second way to protect newborns alongside the infant monoclonal antibody nirsevimab. U.S. approval limited use to 32 through 36 weeks' gestation and timed vaccination to the RSV season, partly because of a numerical, nonsignificant imbalance in preterm births, so the choice between maternal vaccine and infant antibody is now a standard prenatal conversation.

hero_findings.headline: Efficacy against severe RSV lower respiratory tract illness in infants within 90 days (99.5% CI 40.6 to 96.3)
Severe RSV illness by 90 days in infants of placebo recipients, versus 6 after maternal vaccination
Efficacy against severe RSV illness still present at 180 days (97.58% CI 44.3 to 84.1)
Efficacy against RSV illness of any severity at 90 days: did not meet the success criterion

RSVpreF vaccine administered during pregnancy was effective against medically attended severe RSV-associated lower respiratory tract illness in infants, and no safety concerns were identified.
